hero.headline: Judge orders Martin County teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments reinstated with back pay
hero.body:
A Florida judge has ruled that Matthew Theobald, a social studies teacher and union president at Martin County School District, must be reinstated to his position and receive back pay after being suspended over comments he posted on his personal Facebook page. Theobald, who had worked in the district for 17 years, was removed from his job in September 2025 following the posts about Charlie Kirk. Superintendent Michael Maine recommended his termination in October, and the teacher remained suspended without pay until an administrative law judge reviewed the case in April.

The Division of Administrative Hearings judge cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling in his decision. That ruling determined that disciplining a teacher for personal social media posts made off school grounds, using personal equipment, and with no student involvement violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge found that Theobald's situation involved circumstances very similar to those in the appellate case, making the school district's disciplinary action unconstitutional.

The judge also determined that Martin County School District failed to follow its own progressive discipline policy. Rather than moving through standard corrective steps like counseling, reprimands, and other lesser actions, the school board went directly to suspending Theobald without pay and recommending his termination. By skipping these procedural requirements, the district compounded its legal violations. Based on these findings, the judge ordered the school district to reinstate Theobald and provide him with back pay and benefits.

This case reflects a broader trend of disciplinary actions against educators and public employees across the country following comments about Charlie Kirk's death. Similar situations have resulted in significant financial consequences for employers. In a related case last month, a Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission biologist who was fired over a personal social media post about Kirk received a settlement of $485,000. These rulings and settlements underscore growing legal recognition that public employees cannot be disciplined for lawful personal speech made outside of work on their own time, particularly when such speech does not affect their job duties or involve students.

cards.headline: Florida TaxWatch forecasts economic slowdown with unemployment rising to 4.8%
cards.body:
Florida TaxWatch released a new analysis showing the state's economic and population growth will decelerate over the next decade amid challenging economic headwinds. The report indicates that maintaining the strong economic expansion Florida has experienced in recent years will become increasingly difficult. The unemployment rate has climbed every month in 2026, reaching 4.8% in April according to FloridaCommerce, the state's economic development bureau. This rate exceeds the national unemployment rate of 4.3%, signaling labor market weakness ahead.

While gross domestic product growth will remain strong and outpace the rest of the nation through 2030, the labor market presents a greater concern. The report projects that GDP growth will experience some sluggish phases next year, with unemployment and income growth rates both expected to decline. The analysis acknowledged that the full economic consequences of the war with Iran remain uncertain. Despite these headwinds, Florida's economy expanded to $1.87 trillion in 2025, and projections suggest expansion will continue into coming years due to expected population growth in 2026. According to the report, if Florida were an independent nation, its economic output would rank 13th globally.

Population growth, while continuing, will occur at a slower pace than recent years. Currently, Florida experiences a net migration of 895 more people moving into the state daily than leaving. That daily net influx is projected to drop to 689 over the next decade. Florida's population, now approximately 23 million people, is expected to grow by roughly 2.3 million by 2035. Jeff Kottkamp, CEO and President of TaxWatch, stated that "Florida's economy is now set to return to pre-pandemic growth rates over the next five years, after experiencing high economic growth in the past three years."

Despite the projected slowdown, some optimistic signs emerge from the forecast. Kottkamp noted that while Florida entered 2026 with strong growth trends and ranked number one in terms of economic strength, the organization continues to question whether the state's impressive growth rate can sustain over the coming years. He added that "Florida's economic outlook, while hampered by current global events, still reflects some of the signs for optimism it gleamed at the end of 2025." The economic forecast represents part of TaxWatch's quarterly analysis of factors influencing Florida's economy, providing a comprehensive view of both challenges and opportunities ahead.

cards.headline: Indian River County's Ixora Park community receives $1 million federal grant for sewage system upgrade
cards.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will help fund a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system in the Ixora Park community, affecting over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system.
cards.body:
Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced a $1 million federal grant Wednesday to help fund a $20.8 million sewage system upgrade in the Ixora Park community of Indian River County. The Member Community Project Funding will address a failing sewer system affecting over 230 homes that risks contaminating environmental resources. Haridopolos said the federal support ensures health and safety by rehabilitating infrastructure while protecting the Indian River Lagoon, a designated federal resource.

The Ixora Park community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon, one of the most diverse estuaries in the country. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted that environmental conditions make the upgrade critical, as the high water table means significant rainfall flows underground through the subsurface. The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure to reduce discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Haridopolos added that the improvements extend beyond environmental protection, as replacing the aging systems also increases the taxable value of homes in the area.

Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County noted the lagoon has changed dramatically over twenty years, with nobody swimming in it anymore. He explained that the water table is so high and there is so much rain that it all flows underground through the subsurface. Haridopolos said the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, as replacing the infrastructure improves both water quality and the taxable value of homes.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds proposes damage caps to end Florida's medical malpractice free kill law
cards.teaser: The Naples Republican gubernatorial candidate says capping damages could unlock a compromise on Florida's unique prohibition against certain wrongful death lawsuits.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds, a Naples Republican running for Governor, proposed capping damages as a solution to Florida's "free kill" law, which bars unmarried adults over 25 and their parents from suing for pain and suffering in wrongful death medical malpractice cases. Florida is the only state with such a restriction. "Caps is where it's going to begin and end," Donalds said in response to audience questions at a Hardee County event this week. He emphasized that policymakers need to be mindful of medical malpractice impacts, which reflect in the cost of care. "I want to make sure that if something goes wrong on the operating table, that the family has an ability to be made whole, because every life is sacred," he said.

The "free kill" law was signed by Gov. Lawton Chiles in 1990 as part of an expansion to the state's Wrongful Death Act. Lawmakers in recent years have attempted to remove the restriction, but those measures have not become law. Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed a bill in 2025 that would have allowed recovery without an upper statutory limit, citing concerns about "jackpot justice." Donalds expressed optimism that new legislative leadership may find a balanced solution that allows families to be made whole without placing excessive burden on medical providers.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue battles roof fire at Dillard's in Jensen Beach
cards.teaser: Multiple Martin County Fire Rescue units battled a roof fire at the Dillard's department store in Jensen Beach Wednesday night.
cards.body: Multiple Martin County Fire Rescue units are battling a roof fire at the Dillard's department store in Jensen Beach. The call came in just before 9 p.m. and residents are asked to avoid the area as firefighters work to extinguish the fire. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the fire appears to have started on the west side of the mall near Dillard's and looks to be caused by possible electrical issues or lightning.

cards.body:

Families affected by the diagnoses are looking for potential connections or environmental factors that might explain the cluster of cases. The new diagnoses have renewed concerns among St. Lucie County residents about possible causes.

The ongoing pattern of brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County has prompted families to seek information about potential links between the diagnoses. Community members continue to question whether there are common factors contributing to the cancers.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County property tax debate centers on public safety spending
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo says most taxpayer dollars collected in the county go to public safety, with $1.1 billion for the sheriff and approximately $700 million for fire rescue.
cards.body:
When Palm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo confronted state Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia about cutting property taxes, public safety spending became a central point of dispute. Abruzzo said most taxpayer dollars collected in the county support public safety, with $1.1 billion going to the sheriff and approximately $700 million to fire rescue. "If you add up all our departments there is only $609 million when you remove the first responders, and the $609 million is what he is essentially attacking," Abruzzo said Tuesday.

Ingoglia came to Boca Raton this week to announce Palm Beach County was overspending by $443 million and to promote a referendum this fall that would raise the Homestead Exemption to $250,000 in 2027 and $500,000 in 2028. Abruzzo noted that new revenue of approximately $73 million this year is already being absorbed by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, which is requesting a $94 million increase. The Palm Beach Sheriff's Office responded in a statement that ensuring safety and security is a government priority and hopes law enforcement funding remains a priority. Former Florida State Senator Jeff Brandes warned that sheriff's offices and police departments may need to find alternative funding sources if tax reform passes.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach residents fight to preserve Nickels Forest as developer proposes 72 townhomes
cards.teaser: Boynton Beach residents are continuing their fight to preserve a nearly 10-acre forest along city and county lines, pushing back against a developer's proposal to build 72 townhomes near their neighborhood.
cards.body:
Boynton Beach residents are fighting to preserve a nearly 10-acre forest near Quentin Avenue and Nickels Boulevard, pushing back against a developer's proposal to build 72 townhomes. The land, divided by a city-county boundary line, is home to gopher tortoises, grey foxes and other wildlife. Residents say the two adjoining parcels represent some of the last remaining green space in the area. Michael Zwierzyna, who has lived in the neighborhood since 2020, said the forest has become part of his family's daily routine. "My children love being able to see a tortoise," Zwierzyna said. He is among residents who gather every Wednesday to discuss developments on the land.

Developers with Mizner Global purchased nearly 10 acres of county land in March 2025 and sought to buy the city's portion for $5 million, a move the city halted. The current proposal of 72 townhomes represents a revision from an earlier plan proposing 34 single-family homes. During Tuesday's city commission meeting, Commissioner Thomas Turkin voiced support for preservation, saying the city should examine where it will draw the line on preserving land. Resident Susan Oyer acknowledged that developers have permission to build the 34 single-family homes but said residents prefer full preservation. Residents have raised concerns about trees disturbed without proper permits. The group's Change.org petition has gathered more than 1,500 signatures.

cards.headline: Jupiter surgeon uses opioid-free recovery protocol for joint replacement patients
cards.teaser: Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, uses the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocol combined with his own proprietary method to help patients recover from joint replacement surgery without ever touching an opioid.
cards.body:
Andrew Noble, an orthopedic surgeon at Jupiter Medical Center, is using the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol combined with his own proprietary method to help patients recover from joint replacement surgery without opioids. The protocol combines robotics for minimally invasive surgery, targeted numbing, and a timed schedule of non-opioid medications taken before, during, and after surgery. "Instead of chasing pain, it's a way of trying to stay ahead of pain, and have less pain afterwards with less need for opioids," Noble said. Patient April Stubbs recovered from knee replacement surgery without opioids using this approach. "I never had to touch the more serious pain medications. The opioids never even had to take any," Stubbs said.

At Reprieve Recovery in Jupiter, Chief Marketing Officer Daniel Warren emphasized that patients are often unaware of the physical effects of opioid medications taken during surgical recovery. "They'll take a substance for two weeks, and they'll feel uncomfortable, or they'll go through withdrawals, and they don't even know why," Warren said. Warren got sober at Reprieve Recovery eight years ago and has spent the last seven years working there to help others do the same. Patients interested in opioid-free recovery can ask their doctor if the ERAS protocol is an option for them.

hero.headline: Jupiter approves fire assessment fee for new fire rescue department starting October 1
hero.teaser: Jupiter's town council approved a fire assessment fee to help fund the town's new fire rescue department, which begins service Oct. 1. The fee will cover about 8% of the total cost of the department.
hero.body:
Jupiter's town council has approved a fire assessment fee to fund the town's new fire rescue department, set to begin operations on October 1. The assessment will replace the current county fire fee that residents see on their tax bills each year. According to the town's funding plan, property taxes will cover 84% of the department's costs, with the assessment fee covering 8% and EMS transport fees making up the remaining 8%.

Finance Director Scott Reynolds highlighted the financial benefits of this new arrangement for property owners. "The immediate savings for property owners, we've been talking about this for three years, starting at $25 million so right out of the gate, a $10 million savings to the residents," Reynolds said. The town sent informational letters to 30,000 homes to explain the new fee structure to residents. However, the change has generated some confusion among property owners. Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged this confusion, noting that the town has not previously implemented a non ad-valorem assessment. To help residents understand the impact, the town created an online calculator where property owners can determine their potential savings under the new system.

Despite the overall council approval, Mayor Jim Kuretski cast the sole dissenting vote against the funding structure. His concerns centered on inconsistencies in how the assessment is calculated for different property types. "Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches. Townhomes and condos are not," Kuretski said. This difference in assessment methodology raises questions about fairness across the community's various residential categories.

Some residents have also raised concerns about the long-term implications of the assessment fee. While the immediate savings appear substantial, questions remain about whether the fee could increase in future years as the department's needs evolve. The town's effort to communicate the change through direct mail and an online calculator represents an attempt to address resident concerns and clarify the transition from the current county fire fee system to the new Jupiter fire rescue department funding model.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach approves 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach through 2043
cards.teaser: The Lake Worth Beach City Commission unanimously approved a 10-year lease extension for Benny's on the Beach, pushing the pier restaurant's lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years.
cards.body:
Dylan Lipton, Benny's owner, defended the extension by pointing to the restaurant's decades-long presence in the community. Lipton said the restaurant employs more than 100 local residents, invests $1 million annually in maintenance, repairs, utilities, and improvements, and serves as a major tourism driver. The restaurant had requested the maximum 30-year term allowed under city rules, but the commission approved a 10-year extension instead, pushing the lease from January 2033 to February 2043 with a 5% rent increase every two years.

Not everyone supported the move. Resident Jenny Powell questioned the timing and what residents stood to gain, saying she could not think of any benefit to residents for extending the lease. Resident Kim Stokes raised concerns about unequal treatment, comparing how the commission handled Benny's lease to its recent discussions about the Beach Club. Resident Nancy Udell warned the commission against limiting the options of future elected officials, noting that the pier is a valuable asset owned by the people. Commissioner Christopher Serafinchan was the extension's lead advocate on the dais, calling Benny's the city's top-earning tenant. Mayor Betty Resch framed the extension as a matter of stability for a long-standing community business. The commission approved the 10-year extension unanimously.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties to continue near sea turtle nesting area with new lighting rules
cards.teaser: Weekend beach dance parties will continue at Jupiter's sea turtle nesting area with lighting adjustments. The Town of Jupiter convened a meeting Wednesday afternoon bringing together local, county, and state stakeholders along with representatives from Loggerhead Marinelife Center.
cards.body:
The Town of Jupiter held a meeting Wednesday afternoon at the police department bringing together local, county, and state stakeholders along with representatives from Loggerhead Marinelife Center to address concerns about weekend beach dance parties. The meeting lasted about an hour and a half. Afterward, representatives from Happy Beach Dancing said the gathering was productive and that the parties will continue with adjustments. "We're going to continue, just a couple of adjustments. Beautiful," said Foreli of Happy Beach Dancing.

The adjustments focus on reducing lighting during the events to avoid disturbing nesting sea turtles. Previously, some had called for moving the dancing away from the area entirely during nesting season. Happy Beach Dancing said the group will be at Beach Access 55 again this Saturday. The Town of Jupiter and Loggerhead Marinelife Center both responded to the new decision.

cards.headline: Floridians say gas prices over $1 more would tank summer road trips
cards.teaser: A new survey shows two out of three Floridians say higher prices could tank their summer road trips this year as gas prices are starting to fall.
cards.body:
A new survey by RV Windshield Replacement reveals that two out of three Floridians say higher gas prices could "tank" their summer road trips this year. The survey found that Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel is off. When WPTV Anchor Hollani Davis asked drivers at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach if they could afford it, one driver responded, "No. There is no way."

The survey found 68% of Florida drivers agree shorter state trips might be most doable, but some say even that could be tough to pull off. One WPTV viewer shared that instead of visiting Orlando every two weeks, they now go once a month or sometimes skip a month because of gas prices. Another driver told WPTV, "I mean, no one can unless you're rich," when discussing the financial strain of higher fuel costs on vacation plans.

hero.headline: Portugal fans pack Loxahatchee club to watch World Cup opening match
hero.teaser: Dozens of Portugal supporters filled the Portuguese American Culture Society of Palm Beach County in Loxahatchee to watch the team's first World Cup match together.
hero.body:
Dozens of Portugal supporters packed the Portuguese American Culture Society of Palm Beach County in Loxahatchee to watch the team's World Cup opening match, surrounded by Portuguese beer, wine, and food from the Iberian Peninsula. Vic Piorro, treasurer of the club, said the energy in the room reflected how deeply soccer is woven into Portuguese identity. "In Portugal, you have soccer, that's all there is. So it's very much part of our culture and our tradition," Piorro said. The club has served as a gathering place for the local Portuguese community since 1981. "It really started out just as a place for us to gather and speak our language, eat our food, observe our traditions and our culture, and it's grown into much more than that," Piorro said.

Among the fans in attendance were Jonathan Reinoso and his father, Johnny-Lee Reinoso, who left work early to make it to the club in time for kickoff. Jonathan has been a superfan since childhood. When the Portuguese national team set down roots in Palm Beach Gardens for their practice facility, his father got his son a chance to meet the team, including Cristiano Ronaldo. "I've been a fan my whole life, and when I just met him, it was just a dream, like I was in complete shock," Jonathan said. Even though the game ended in a tie, the night was still a celebration for the Reinoso family and everyone at the club.

Finance Director Scott Reynolds said the move represents significant savings for property owners, noting "$10 million savings to the residents" immediately, after discussions spanning three years that began with "$25 million" in potential savings.

Mayor Jim Kuretski was the lone no vote on the funding structure, raising concerns about how the assessment is calculated across different property types. Single family homes are being assessed based on total square footage including garages and porches, while townhomes and condos are not, Kuretski said. The town sent letters to 30,000 homes explaining the fee. Town of Jupiter spokesperson Mariana DiNunzio acknowledged confusion from the change. The town has established an online calculator where residents can see their potential savings.

cards.headline: Promise Fund to offer free mammogram screenings in Jupiter and West Palm Beach next month
cards.teaser: Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through events hosted by Promise Fund.
cards.body:
Women in Palm Beach County will have two opportunities next month to receive free mammogram screenings through events hosted by Promise Fund, a South Florida nonprofit focused on increasing survivorship from breast and cervical cancer. The organization will hold free Mammography Screening Days on July 11 in Jupiter and July 12 in West Palm Beach, offered in partnership with Florida Mobile Mammography, HealthyMe, the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, Origin Church, the Florida Department of Health and Monarch Health Services. The first event is scheduled for July 11 from 8 a.m. on Indiantown Road in Jupiter, while the second will take place July 12 from 9 a.m. in West Palm Beach. Appointments are required for both events, and those interested can register by calling 877-427-7664.

Promise Fund serves women throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Martin counties who are uninsured, underinsured or have limited access to health care. The organization has reached more than 145,000 women across South Florida through education and advocacy efforts. More than 27,000 women have received access to screenings, diagnostics and care through its programs, and 286 women diagnosed with cancer have received assistance navigating treatment. The nonprofit currently operates 4 co-located screening programs in Palm Beach and Broward counties and is seeking funding to establish a similar program in Martin County.

cards.headline: Floridians say gas prices above $4 could cancel summer road trips
cards.teaser: Two out of three Floridians say higher prices could tank their summer road trips this year as gas prices start to fall.
cards.body:
Gas prices are starting to fall just in time as a new survey shows two out of three Floridians say higher prices could "tank" their summer road trips this year. A survey by RV Windshield Replacement set out to gauge how costs are reshaping vacation plans. Florida drivers polled say if gas prices go up another $1.01, their summer road trip travel is off. "No. There is no way," said one driver at a gas station on 45th Street in West Palm Beach.

The survey found 68% of Florida drivers agree shorter state trips might be most doable, but some say even that could be tough to pull off. One viewer explained that instead of traveling to Orlando every two weeks, they are now considering going once a month or sometimes skipping a month altogether because of gas prices. "I mean, no one can unless you're rich," said another driver.

cards.headline: Erling Haaland scores twice in World Cup debut as Norway beats Iraq 4-1
cards.teaser: Erling Haaland scored twice and added an assist in his World Cup debut as Norway topped Iraq 4-1 in Group I play.
cards.body:
Erling Haaland made his World Cup debut memorable by scoring twice and adding an assist as Norway defeated Iraq 4-1 in Group I. The Manchester City striker's performance helped Norway start their World Cup campaign with a convincing victory. Haaland's two goals and playmaking ability showcased why he is considered one of the most dangerous forwards in international football.

The match marked Norway's opening game of the tournament. Iraq struggled to contain Haaland and the Norwegian attack throughout the contest. The 4-1 result gives Norway three points in Group I as they look to advance from the group stage.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge with prizes through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is hosting its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge called Unearth a Story, running now through July 31 with free activities, incentives, and grand prizes for all ages.
hero.body:
Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen said the program offers free activities, incentives, and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log, and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs will also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5-11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain, or dino pencil. Teens ages 12-17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip, or notebook.

Each branch is hosting special events from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. McMullen added that families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach offers adults-only nights and free dad admission this summer
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach is hosting several special events this summer targeting different audiences. Adults Night returns with music, glow items, and exclusive access for guests 21 and older to enjoy the slides, lazy river, and wave pool under the stars. Elliott Russell, the park's director of marketing and sales, confirmed the event's return. The park is also offering free admission for dads on June 20-21 during Father's Day weekend, according to Greg Fuller, the park's general manager.

Beyond entertainment, Rapids Water Park is participating in a global water safety initiative. On June 25, the park will join Live Like Jake and worldwide participants for the World's Largest Swim Lesson, a coordinated effort to raise awareness about water safety. The park, located at 6566 N. Military Trail in Riviera Beach, is open daily with various ticket packages. New viral treats, including specialty funnel cakes, will be available this season.

hero.headline: Florida TaxWatch forecasts economic slowdown with unemployment rising to 4.8%
hero.body:
Florida TaxWatch released a new analysis showing the state's economic and population growth will decelerate over the next decade amid challenging economic headwinds. The report indicates that maintaining the strong economic expansion Florida has experienced in recent years will become increasingly difficult. The unemployment rate has climbed every month in 2026, reaching 4.8% in April according to FloridaCommerce, the state's economic development bureau. This rate exceeds the national unemployment rate of 4.3%, signaling labor market weakness ahead.

While gross domestic product growth will remain strong and outpace the rest of the nation through 2030, the labor market presents a greater concern. The report projects that GDP growth will experience some sluggish phases next year, with unemployment and income growth rates both expected to decline. The analysis acknowledged that the full economic consequences of the war with Iran remain uncertain. Despite these headwinds, Florida's economy expanded to $1.87 trillion in 2025, and projections suggest expansion will continue into coming years due to expected population growth in 2026. According to the report, if Florida were an independent nation, its economic output would rank 13th globally.

Population growth, while continuing, will occur at a slower pace than recent years. Currently, Florida experiences a net migration of 895 more people moving into the state daily than leaving. That daily net influx is projected to drop to 689 over the next decade. Florida's population, now approximately 23 million people, is expected to grow by roughly 2.3 million by 2035. Jeff Kottkamp, CEO and President of TaxWatch, stated that "Florida's economy is now set to return to pre-pandemic growth rates over the next five years, after experiencing high economic growth in the past three years."

Despite the projected slowdown, some optimistic signs emerge from the forecast. Kottkamp noted that while Florida entered 2026 with strong growth trends and ranked number one in terms of economic strength, the organization continues to question whether the state's impressive growth rate can sustain over the coming years. He added that "Florida's economic outlook, while hampered by current global events, still reflects some of the signs for optimism it gleamed at the end of 2025." The economic forecast represents part of TaxWatch's quarterly analysis of factors influencing Florida's economy, providing a comprehensive view of both challenges and opportunities ahead.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds proposes damage caps to end Florida's medical malpractice free kill law
cards.teaser: The Naples Republican gubernatorial candidate says capping damages could unlock a compromise on Florida's unique prohibition against certain wrongful death lawsuits.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds, a Naples Republican running for Governor, proposed capping damages as a solution to Florida's "free kill" law, which bars unmarried adults over 25 and their parents from suing for pain and suffering in wrongful death medical malpractice cases. Florida is the only state with such a restriction. "Caps is where it's going to begin and end," Donalds said in response to audience questions at a Hardee County event this week. He emphasized that policymakers need to be mindful of medical malpractice impacts, which reflect in the cost of care. "I want to make sure that if something goes wrong on the operating table, that the family has an ability to be made whole, because every life is sacred," he said.

The "free kill" law was signed by Gov. Lawton Chiles in 1990 as part of an expansion to the state's Wrongful Death Act. Lawmakers in recent years have attempted to remove the restriction, but those measures have not become law. Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed a bill in 2025 that would have allowed recovery without an upper statutory limit, citing concerns about "jackpot justice." Donalds expressed optimism that new legislative leadership may find a balanced solution that allows families to be made whole without placing excessive burden on medical providers.

cards.headline: Florida Professional Firefighters endorse Ashley Moody for U.S. Senate
cards.teaser: The union backed the Plant City Republican as she seeks election to the seat in November after being appointed last year.
cards.body:
The Florida Professional Firefighters union has endorsed Ashley Moody, the Plant City Republican who stands for election to the U.S. Senate in November. FPF President Wayne "Bernie" Bernoska said Moody "has been a steadfast supporter of Florida's firefighters and paramedics throughout her career in public service." He noted her record as Florida Attorney General and in the U.S. Senate, stating "she has consistently demonstrated a commitment to public safety and to the men and women who answer the call every day." The firefighters' association previously supported Moody when she successfully ran for re-election as Florida Attorney General in 2022. Governor Ron DeSantis appointed Moody to her U.S. Senate seat last year.

Moody said the endorsement recognizes her commitment to first responders. "Our firefighters run toward danger so the rest of us can run to safety, and for over 80 years, the Florida Professional Firefighters organization has represented that brotherhood with distinction," she said. The organization highlighted Moody's legislative work in Washington, specifically her introduction of the Homes for Every Local Protector, Educator, and Responder (HELPER) Act. The legislation would establish a Federal Housing Administration program to provide mortgage assistance to first responders, including firefighters, and teachers.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds warns homestead exemption amendment could shift taxes to special assessments
cards.teaser: The gubernatorial candidate says the constitutional amendment may change how local governments raise revenue rather than provide meaningful relief.
cards.body:
Gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds says a constitutional amendment that would raise Florida's homestead exemption may just end up changing how local governments get their revenue rather than provide meaningful relief for Floridians. HJR 1-F would create a $250,000 exemption on Florida's primary residences, but does not change language regarding assessments for special benefits. The Naples Congressman believes that could create a tax shift. "My concern with the amendment is that it allows for non-ad valorem assessments. So if you actually read the amendment, non-ad valorem assessments would be allowed," Donalds said. Special assessments fund a wide variety of projects, including street lighting, fire and rescue, stormwater and drainage, private security in some areas, landscaping, road and canal maintenance, beach renourishment, and community development.

The Office of Economic and Demographic Research estimates that a total of $11.86 billion would eventually be extracted from local budgets per year. Larger urban counties would face the biggest hit in raw dollars. Miami-Dade would experience a $445 million revenue decrease as soon as Fiscal Year 2028-29. Hillsborough could lose $353 million, Broward roughly $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million by the same point. If approved by at least 60% of voters in November, the constitutional amendment would lift homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds says he has no interest in returning to Washington after Governor race
cards.teaser: The Naples Republican told a Hardee County crowd he is focused on Florida and does not plan to seek the presidency.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds hasn't secured his party's nomination to run for Governor yet, but he continues fielding questions about higher political ambitions. When asked about a potential national campaign this week at a campaign event in Hardee County, the Naples Republican firmly dismissed the idea. "Right now, I'm focused on being Governor of Florida. I don't believe in planning politics. I think you worry about the thing in front of you, and you do that job," Donalds said. "To be honest, I really don't have any interest in going back to Washington, D.C. And this state is home to me."

His messaging on the topic has been consistent. Earlier this month on "HotCakes Hot Takes," Donalds explained his approach to timing in politics, saying he focuses on his current responsibilities rather than hypothetical future positions. Donalds would not follow the path of Florida governors Reubin Askew, Jeb Bush, Ron DeSantis, or Bob Graham, all of whom ran for President. DeSantis notably launched his presidential campaign months after being sworn in for a second term. Polymarket currently gives Donalds a 0.8% chance of winning the GOP nomination in two years.

The Super Speeder law applies to motorists who drive at excessive speeds above posted limits. Violators face additional fines and potential license suspensions beyond standard speeding citations.

The Port St. Lucie case represents enforcement of the state statute designed to deter dangerous high speed driving on Florida roadways. Motorcyclists are subject to the same Super Speeder penalties as other vehicle operators.

The ongoing pattern of brain cancer cases in St. Lucie County has prompted families to seek information about potential links between the diagnoses. Community members continue to question whether there are common factors contributing to the cancers.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce teen killed in shooting after Instagram firearm exchange arrangement
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce teenager was killed in a shooting that followed a planned firearm exchange arranged through Instagram, according to police.

A Fort Pierce teenager was killed in a shooting that followed a planned firearm exchange arranged through Instagram, according to police. The shooting occurred when the teen was riding a bicycle in Fort Pierce.

Fort Pierce police said the fatal shooting resulted from a gun exchange that had been arranged on social media. Investigators characterized the incident as unprecedented in the area, with one official stating this type of social media arranged firearm transaction leading to violence is a first for the department.

The teen victim was on a bicycle at the time of the shooting. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the planned exchange and how it turned deadly.

Authorities are working to determine who was involved in the shooting and what led to the fatal violence during the attempted transaction. The investigation into the Instagram arranged gun exchange continues.

hero.headline: $1 million federal grant funds Ixora Park sewage system upgrade in Indian River County
hero.teaser: A $1 million federal grant will fund a major sewage system upgrade in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at.
hero.body:
A $1 million federal grant will help fund a major sewage system upgrade in the Ixora Park community in Indian River County, Congressman Mike Haridopolos announced at a press conference Wednesday afternoon. The Member Community Project Funding will support a $20.8 million project to retrofit the sewage system affecting over 230 homes that currently rely on a failing sewer system risking contamination of environmental resources. Haridopolos said the federal support ensures health and safety to the community by rehabilitating infrastructure while protecting the Indian River Lagoon, a designated federal resource and one of the most diverse estuaries in the country.

The Ixora Park community sits adjacent to the County South Relief Canal, which discharges into the Indian River Lagoon. Keith Drewett of the Clean Water Coalition of Indian River County said the lagoon is dramatically different from twenty years ago in terms of fishing and swimming, with nobody swimming in the lagoon anymore. The Clean Water Coalition identified the upgrade as critical because the water table is high and heavy rain flows underground through the subsurface. The project will replace aging sewer infrastructure and reduce discharges of nitrogen and phosphorus into the lagoon. Haridopolos noted the benefits extend beyond environmental protection, as replacing the failing systems improves water quality and increases the taxable value of homes in the community.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach residents fight developer's plan for 72 townhomes at Nickels Forest
cards.teaser: Boynton Beach residents are continuing their fight to preserve a nearly 10-acre forest along city and county lines, pushing back against a developer's proposal to build 72 townhomes near their neighborhood.
cards.body:
Boynton Beach residents are fighting a developer's proposal to build 72 townhomes on nearly 10 acres of forest near Quentin Avenue and Nickels Boulevard. Developers with Mizner Global purchased the county-owned land in March 2025 and also sought to buy the adjacent city-owned parcel for $5 million, a purchase the city blocked. The two parcels are separated by a city-county line and are home to gopher tortoises, grey foxes and other wildlife. Michael Zwierzyna, who has lived in the neighborhood since 2020, said his children enjoy seeing tortoises on the property. A group of residents meets every Wednesday to discuss developments on the land.

During Tuesday's city commission meeting, commissioners agreed to discuss the proposal at a later date. Commissioner Thomas Turkin expressed support for preservation, saying the city's land should be preserved and that growth can happen responsibly. Resident Susan Oyer acknowledged that the developer has legal permission to build 34 single-family homes under the earlier proposal but said residents want full preservation. Residents have raised concerns about trees they say were disturbed without proper permits, with stop work order signs visible on the property. A Change.org petition opposing the development has gathered more than 1,500 signatures.
